title: Detection Strategy for Spearphishing Voice across OS platforms
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Spearphishing Voice across OS plat...
summary: This strategy detects voice phishing, where an adversary telephones a member of staff while pretending to be support, a vendor or an executive, and talks them into resetting a factor, approving a prompt or installing remote access software. The technique matters because the human conversation carries no malicious file and no unusual process, so the initial contact is invisible to endpoint and mail controls, and the real damage happens in identity and helpdesk systems moments later. Detection therefore depends on voice platform call detail records, identity provider audit logs for authentication method and device changes, and endpoint process creation for remote support utilities. The main way it fails is attribution and scale: staff take vendor calls all day, so any rule must be built on a short sequence of call plus high impact action and tuned to the roles that attackers impersonate.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for phone based trickery that leads to a real change in an account. An attacker calls someone and pretends to be from the information technology team or a supplier. Then they ask for a code, a password reset or a remote control session. The rule joins the call with the account change that follows.
beginner.whyItMatters: The call carries no bad file, so mail filters see nothing. The attacker uses trust and time pressure instead of software. The action they ask for is often allowed for the real employee. The damage then shows up in the identity system. Alerts must be built from those records, not from the phone call alone.
howItWorks: A call arrives from an outside number to a member of staff.
The voice system or phone platform writes a call detail record with both numbers and the time.
Shortly after, the identity system records a change such as a factor reset or a new device.
The rule links calls and identity changes that happen inside a short window.
It also checks whether the staff member installed a remote support tool in that window.
Only the combination of a call and a high impact action raises an alert for review.
beginner.example: Think of a bank where a thief calls the counter and says he is from the fraud team. The call is not written in the door log. But the teller resetting a password for him and adding a new payee right after the call would be noticed. Phone tricks work the same way, so you watch what the call sets in motion.
takeaways: The phone call leaves little evidence, so watch the action it causes.
A call plus an authentication change in a short window is the useful signal.
Tune the rule to roles that attackers like to impersonate, such as helpdesk and finance.

objectives: Describe voice phishing and why it leaves few technical traces.
Explain why detection has to combine call records with identity and endpoint events.
Identify the identity changes that attackers usually request during a call.
Correlate a call detail record with an authentication method change in a short window.
Recognise remote support tool installation as a common outcome of a voice approach.
Describe how to scope the rule to roles that are frequently impersonated.
dataSources: Voice platform or private branch exchange call detail records giving calling number, called number, direction and duration
Identity provider audit logs recording authentication method resets, new device registrations and password changes with the source address
Sysmon event 1 process creation records for remote support and screen sharing software with command line arguments
Helpdesk ticketing records showing identity verification steps and the channel used to request a change
Endpoint detection file creation records for newly installed remote access agents in user profile directories
logic: The pattern is an inbound external call to a specific member of staff followed within a short window by a high impact identity action or the installation of remote access software involving that person or an account they support. The fields that must be correlated are the calling number, the called number and its owner, the call start time and duration, the identity operation performed, the actor and target accounts, the source address of the operation, and any process creation for remote support tooling on the same host. The malicious case usually shows a first time external caller, a call to a helpdesk or finance extension, then a factor reset or remote session started minutes later, with the requestor unable to name a matching ticket. The benign case is a genuine vendor engineer calling about an open case and asking the customer to join a support session, an internal support callback after a ticket, or a sales call that ends with no system change.
pseudoQuery:
# title: External Call Then MFA Reset or Remote Support Start
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection_call:
#     event_type: 'call_detail'
#     direction: 'inbound'
#     caller|not_cidr: '10[.]0[.]0[.]0/8'
#   selection_identity:
#     OperationName|contains: 'Reset authentication method'
#   selection_remote:
#     Image|endswith: '\quickassist.exe'
#   filter_vendor:
#     caller|in: 'approved_vendor_numbers'
#   condition: selection_call and (selection_identity or selection_remote) and not filter_vendor
# level: medium
falsePositives: A genuine software vendor engineer who calls about an open case and asks the customer to join a remote support session
An internal service desk callback to a user who reported a problem, followed by a legitimate factor reset
A sales or partner call to a finance team member that happens to fall near a scheduled password change
A customer support team that uses a remote support tool many times a day for legitimate troubleshooting
tuningNotes: Start by enriching call detail records with the called extension owner and their role, then scope the first version to helpdesk, finance, executive assistants and privileged administrators, where a successful voice approach has the largest effect. Maintain an approved vendor number list with an expiry date for each entry and filter those calls only while an open support case exists, so a re-used or spoofed number loses its pass. Set the correlation window from your own data, usually thirty to sixty minutes, and require the call to be the first contact from that number in the last thirty days. The coverage you lose by narrowing to a few roles and first time callers is a patient attacker who calls several times to build rapport, so also alert on repeated short calls to the same person from different numbers in one day.
